sectionToMerge.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About Robotic Radical Prostatectomy
sectionToMerge.intro: Clear, patient-friendly answers about robotic radical prostatectomy for prostate cancer, covering how it works, who may qualify, recovery, cost, and access for international patients.

items.a: Robotic radical prostatectomy is a minimally invasive surgery to remove the entire prostate gland and nearby tissue to treat prostate cancer. The surgeon controls robotic arms through a console, using a magnified 3D view and small keyhole incisions instead of one large cut. It is most often performed for cancer confined to the prostate. Whether it suits a patient depends on cancer stage, health, and specialist review.

items.q: How does robotic prostate surgery work?
items.a: During robotic prostate surgery, the surgeon sits at a console and guides tiny instruments through a few small abdominal incisions. A high-definition, magnified 3D camera helps the surgeon see delicate structures clearly, and the robotic arms translate hand movements into precise, steady actions. The prostate is removed and the bladder is reconnected to the urethra. The robot does not act on its own; the surgeon controls every movement.

items.q: What is the difference between robotic and open prostatectomy?
items.a: Robotic prostatectomy uses several small incisions and robotic instruments, while open surgery uses one larger incision to reach the prostate directly. The robotic approach often allows less blood loss, smaller scars, and a shorter hospital stay for selected patients. Both aim to remove the cancer completely. The best option depends on the surgeon's experience, tumour features, and the patient's anatomy, and should be discussed with the treating team.

items.q: Is robotic radical prostatectomy a good treatment for prostate cancer?
items.a: Robotic radical prostatectomy is a well-established option for localised prostate cancer and can offer effective cancer control with a minimally invasive recovery. It may be considered when cancer is confined to the prostate and the patient is fit for surgery. It is not the right choice for everyone, and alternatives like radiation or active surveillance may suit some patients. Final decisions should be made by a qualified oncology and urology team.

items.q: Who is eligible for robotic radical prostatectomy?
items.a: Robotic radical prostatectomy may be suitable for selected men with prostate cancer that appears confined to the prostate and who are healthy enough for surgery and anaesthesia. Eligibility depends on cancer stage, PSA level, Gleason score, imaging, age, and overall health. Men with advanced or widely spread cancer may need other treatments first. A urologist and oncology team decide suitability after reviewing reports and examining the patient.

items.q: What are the risks and side effects of robotic prostatectomy?
items.a: The main possible side effects of robotic prostatectomy are temporary or lasting urinary incontinence and erectile dysfunction, as nerves near the prostate can be affected. Other risks include bleeding, infection, blood clots, and anaesthesia-related complications. Many men regain urinary control and sexual function over months, though recovery varies. Nerve-sparing techniques may help in suitable cases. Risks should be discussed openly with the surgical team before deciding.

items.q: How long does recovery take after robotic prostate surgery?
items.a: Most men leave hospital within one to two days after robotic prostate surgery and return to light activities within two to four weeks. A urinary catheter is usually kept for about one to two weeks. Urinary control and sexual function may take several months to improve. Recovery speed depends on age, fitness, nerve-sparing, and the surgeon's advice. Follow-up PSA tests help monitor for any return of cancer.

items.q: What reports and tests are needed before robotic prostatectomy?
items.a: Before robotic prostatectomy, doctors usually review a prostate biopsy with Gleason score, PSA blood test, and imaging such as MRI, and sometimes a PSMA PET or bone scan to check for spread. General fitness tests, blood work, and an anaesthesia review are also common. These help confirm the cancer stage and whether surgery is appropriate. The exact tests required depend on the hospital and the treating specialist's assessment.

items.q: How much does robotic radical prostatectomy cost?
items.a: The cost of robotic radical prostatectomy varies widely by country, hospital, and individual case, and is often higher than open surgery due to the technology used. Final cost depends on the hospital, diagnosis, tests, surgeon's fees, length of stay, and any complications. Some countries and insurers cover part of the cost. For an accurate estimate, patients should request a written quote from the treating hospital based on their reports.

items.q: Which countries offer robotic radical prostatectomy?
items.a: Robotic radical prostatectomy is available in many countries with advanced surgical centres, including the United States, India, Turkey, Germany, the United Kingdom, Singapore, and several others. Availability depends on hospitals having robotic surgical systems and trained surgeons. Outcomes are strongly linked to surgeon experience rather than location alone. International patients often compare centres for expertise, cost, and support, and should confirm details directly with each hospital.

items.q: Is robotic radical prostatectomy available in India?
items.a: Yes, robotic radical prostatectomy is available at several major hospitals in India that have robotic surgical systems and experienced urologists. India is often chosen by international patients for its combination of advanced technology and comparatively lower cost. Actual suitability, cost, and timing depend on the patient's diagnosis, hospital acceptance, and specialist review. Patients should share their medical reports with the chosen hospital to confirm availability and a personalised estimate.

Nerve-sparing robotic prostatectomy is a technique that tries to preserve the small nerves beside the prostate that control erections, while still removing the cancer. It may be considered when the tumour has not grown into or too close to these nerves. When possible, it can improve the chance of recovering sexual function. It is not suitable for every patient, and safe cancer removal always takes priority over nerve preservation.

items.q: Are there clinical trials for robotic prostate cancer surgery?
items.a: Yes, clinical trials study aspects of robotic prostate surgery such as newer techniques, imaging guidance, and recovery of urinary and sexual function. Trials may be an option for selected patients but cannot guarantee enrolment or benefit. Eligibility is decided after medical record review and investigator assessment, and trials often have strict inclusion and exclusion criteria. Patients interested in trials should discuss suitable options with their oncology and urology team.

items.q: What are the alternatives to robotic radical prostatectomy?
items.a: Alternatives to robotic radical prostatectomy include open or laparoscopic surgery, radiation therapy such as external beam or brachytherapy, and active surveillance for low-risk cancers. Hormone therapy or focal treatments may also be considered in specific situations. The right choice depends on cancer stage, Gleason score, age, health, and personal preferences. These options should be weighed carefully with a qualified oncology team before any final treatment decision is made.

items.q: How can international patients access robotic radical prostatectomy abroad?
items.a: International patients can access robotic radical prostatectomy by sharing their medical reports with a chosen hospital for review, obtaining a treatment plan and cost estimate, and arranging travel and a medical visa. Access depends on hospital acceptance, fitness for travel and surgery, and visa approval, none of which can be guaranteed. Planning follow-up care after returning home is also important and should be discussed with both treating teams.

items.q: How long should international patients stay abroad for the surgery?
items.a: International patients usually plan to stay two to four weeks for robotic radical prostatectomy, allowing time for pre-surgery tests, the operation, catheter removal, and an initial recovery check. The exact duration depends on the hospital's protocol, the patient's recovery, and any complications. Some men may need to stay longer if issues arise. Patients should confirm the expected timeline and follow-up schedule directly with the treating hospital before travelling.

items.q: Should I get a second opinion before robotic prostatectomy?
items.a: A second opinion before robotic prostatectomy is often helpful, as prostate cancer can be treated in several ways and the best option varies by individual. Another specialist can review your biopsy, imaging, and PSA to confirm the diagnosis and discuss whether surgery, radiation, or surveillance suits you. This can improve confidence in the plan. Final treatment decisions should always be made with your treating oncology and urology team.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with robotic radical prostatectomy?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organize medical reports, identify relevant specialists or treatment centers, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, biomarkers, previous treatment, and overall health. CancerFax does not replace doctors or hospitals and cannot guarantee hospital admission, visa approval, or specific treatment outcomes.
